title: O my eyes
hook: the eyes are told the Lord put His light in them, so see Him in all (Anand, the eyes)

segments.voice: Yesterday, jot, and your line, light in the body. Today the Anand turns from the whole body to two small parts of it.

There's a kind of video people love to share: a child getting her first pair of glasses. She puts them on in the optician's chair, looks up at her mother, and her face changes. Then she looks out the window and points. Leaves. She hadn't known trees had separate leaves. Nothing outside had changed. Her sight had. The Anand has a pauri like that moment, spoken straight to the eyes.
screen: `A CHILD'S FIRST GLASSES.` → `TREES HAVE SEPARATE LEAVES.` → `THE WORLD THE SAME, THE SIGHT NEW.`

segments.voice: After the body, Guru Amar Das speaks to the eyes: ae naetrahu mairiho, O my eyes. In paraphrase: the Lord has put His light in you, so look on no one but the Lord. That could sound like a command to stop seeing the world. Read on, and it means nearly the opposite: this whole world you see is the Lord's own form; the Lord's form is what comes into view. So the eyes aren't told to look away from people and places. They're told what they're actually looking at. Then the turn, and it's honest. By the Guru's grace, Guru Amar Das says, I understood: wherever I look, the Lord is one, and there's no other. And the closing line: these eyes were blind, and meeting the True Guru, they received divine sight. The phrase is dib drisat, sight that sees more than surfaces. Like the child in the glasses, the world hasn't changed. The eyes have. Yesterday the light was placed in the body. Today the same light is in the eyes, and with it they're meant to find the same light in everything they see: light looking at light. Sikh teachers draw from this a reason the way you look at someone matters: the stranger on the bus, the person serving you, the one you find hard. The pauri doesn't ask the eyes to close. It asks them to see Him.
screen: `AE NAETRAHU MAIRIHO: O MY EYES.` · `THIS WORLD YOU SEE IS THE LORD'S FORM.` · `THESE EYES WERE BLIND, NOW DIVINE SIGHT.` · `LIGHT LOOKING AT LIGHT.` · then, large: `EYES, SEE HIM.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you'll see today, someone ordinary or someone difficult, and picture their face clearly: the way they stand, the look they get when they're tired. Hold the Anand's line beside the picture, the same light placed in you was placed in them, and breathe, without forcing a feeling. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, with that face in mind.
Naetr, eye. Ae naetrahu mairiho: the Anand tells the eyes the Lord's light is in them, that the world they see is His form, and that meeting the True Guru gives divine sight.
Your line: eyes, see him. The same world, seen with new sight. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: This pauri is part of the full Anand Sahib that many Sikhs recite each morning; seeing the one light in everyone is often given as the ground of Sikh equality, lived out in sangat and langar.

fork.setup: the Anand tells the eyes to look on no one but the Lord. what does it say they should do with the world?
options: see it as the Lord's own form.
fork.reveal: the next lines say the whole world the eyes see is the Lord's form: the eyes don't look away, they see what's there.

original.note: Gurmukhi: naetr, eye; the Anand addresses the eyes as naetrahu, O eyes.

trapdoor: what you thought: O my eyes means look away from the world to see God.
what it means: the light in the eyes is meant to find the same light in everything they see.
what a scholar hears: the pauri closes on dib drisat, divine sight, given by meeting the True Guru; it's the second of the Anand's addresses to parts of the person.
recall: the body, asked what it has done
guess: a lamp lit to read the Granth
a tear shed in deep prayer

chat.says: Does the Anand tell your eyes to stop looking at the world?
options: No: it says this world you see is the Lord's form; the eyes learn what they're seeing.
Yes: it says look only at holy things, and keep your eyes away from other people.
Yes: it says the eyes only mislead, so keeping them closed is the truest prayer.
chat.meaning: Ae naetrahu mairiho: the Lord's light is in the eyes, this world is His form, and meeting the True Guru, blind eyes receive divine sight.

dib drisat.meaning: divine sight, seeing more than surfaces

Guru Amar Das.meaning: the third Guru, who wrote the Anand

sources.ref: Ramkali M3, Anand, the eyes pauri (ae naetrahu mairiho), Ang 922

notes: The eyes pauri paraphrased: the Lord put His light in you, see no other; this world is the Lord's form; by Guru's grace the Lord is one; these eyes were blind, meeting the True Guru they received divine sight (dib drisat). Commonly numbered pauri 36. Confirm numbering, Ang and glosses.
Gurmukhi ਨੇਤ੍ਰ and pronunciation NAY-tr: confirm the spelling and form (the pauri uses ਨੇਤ੍ਰਹੁ).
The 'first glasses' video hook is a general scene, not a specific case.
